title: Where European finance would feel an AI shock first
summary: Which balance sheet would absorb a disappointment in artificial intelligence earnings? The ECB study points first to investment funds that own shares in affected companies. Which financial institutions could lose a critical service even if technology stocks held their value? Banks and funds that depend on the same cloud and model providers. The answers differ because owning a supplier, lending to its customers and using its technology create distinct exposures. The six authors build the evidence for each, drawing on supervisory returns, matched investment funds, business descriptions and securities holdings. The strength of the evidence also differs by channel.

Start with what banks actually do. Across EU enterprises with at least ten people employed, about 20% used at least one AI technology in 2025, up some 6.5 percentage points in a year. Eurostat's definition covers both established machine learning and newer applications. The sector comparisons for US firms in Chart A.1 use a different population and question. They identify intensive users within the US but cannot rank overall US adoption against Europe. Among surveyed euro area banks, use of generative AI rose from 46% to 86% between 2024 and 2025. The share still developing it fell from 38% to 10%. A system used by a legal department qualifies just as one used in a lending decision does. Roughly half of banks already used the technology for legal services or IT operations, rising to around four in five when work under development is included. Credit scoring and risk management were much less advanced. Chart A.2's separate international survey of 61 financial institutions in eight regions still places much activity with autonomous agents in planning or pilots. The available adoption figures cannot tell a credit analyst how much loan underwriting has been delegated.

Asset management offers a different test. Chart A.4 identifies active funds that disclose using machine learning in their investment strategies and matches them with otherwise comparable funds. This is predominantly evidence on established machine learning. Generative AI is more widespread in research and operations than in investment decisions. Among the roughly $10 trillion of sampled assets for which usage information is available, machine-learning funds account for around 15%. Passive strategies are excluded from the matched comparison. The study finds stronger net inflows from January 2023 through September 2026, faster trading and slightly higher returns after fund-level costs in the separate three-year performance comparison. These features could reflect better information processing, but a higher average return says little about simultaneous losses when liquidity is scarce.

For equity funds the authors calculate the probability that a fund falls into its own lower tail on a day when another fund in the same group is already in its lower tail. Looking at daily returns from 1 November 2025 to 26 October 2026, this conditional probability is higher for machine-learning funds than for matched peers across the plotted cutoffs. A joint directional test at the 10th, 15th and 20th percentiles gives p = 0.049. This is group-level evidence over one year. Funds with similar factor exposures can fall together without processing the same news or selling the same asset. If a strategy comes to dominate a narrow market or leveraged funds face simultaneous margin calls, this co-movement could amplify sales. The paper neither observes an AI-induced fire sale nor identifies a general effect of generative tools on asset prices.

An operating disruption follows a different path. In 2025, AWS, Microsoft and Google accounted for an estimated 82% of the broad European cloud market. Together with OpenAI they accounted for an estimated 90% of EU generative AI services. Chart A.5 combines market intelligence, company data and usage indicators. These percentages describe technology markets. The bank sourcing chart counts names reported in supervisory responses, sometimes grouping a platform with its integrated model provider. Contracts with two vendors can still depend on one cloud region or upstream model. The October 2025 AWS outage illustrates how far a regional failure can spread. It generated reports across more than 60 countries, predominantly in consumer-facing services. Financial firms supplied only a small share of reports. Large providers can invest substantially in resilience, but a common outage can complicate simultaneous recovery at several firms even when all remain solvent. The economically relevant measure is continuity of specific services such as payments or access to client accounts, rather than the number of names on a vendor list.

To assess investments, the authors first classify what AI could do to each company's business. They use a specialised language model trained on assessments of a stratified sample of 100,000 firms, then score business descriptions for about 4.5 million companies. One score captures opportunities to improve work or products. The second captures threats to the demand for, price of or role of what the company sells. Relative to the sample average on both axes, around 20% are in the mainly-gains group, 19% have high gains and threats, and 60% rank low on both. Fewer than 0.5% show mainly threats. The very small last group does not imply few potential losers. An above-average opportunity to use AI can coexist with competitors eroding the firm's margins. The scores quantify neither realised adoption nor probabilities of default. Some firms are excluded and the sample composition is global.

Chart A.7 links those scores to euro area bank loans and securities holdings. Where a firm cannot be matched directly but its sector is known, exposure is assigned using the mix for scored firms in that sector. Holding companies, head offices and counterparties without a sector code remain unclassified. Non-banks, particularly investment funds, have substantial equity exposure to AI-intensive firms. Bank lending exposure is more limited, making a revaluation of investments a more immediate loss channel in the authors' assessment. A distinct exercise follows debt funding for 168 companies and their subsidiaries in the AI supply chain. Between the first quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, supply-chain debt rose from approximately 0.7% to 1.2% of investment funds' total debt holdings, while a larger portion of that exposure became concentrated among a few major technology firms. This is a share of the funds' debt portfolio, not their whole balance sheet. More spending financed by bonds or by off-balance-sheet claims on future revenues would earmark tomorrow's cash flows for fixed commitments. Even if banks do little direct lending today, the financing mix determines how a future equity repricing could reach creditors.

For supervisors the evidence favours specific checks over a single adoption target. Explainability is material when a model influences a credit decision. Tested recovery arrangements matter when several critical services use a common supplier. Holdings, contractual leverage and redemption pressure matter when portfolios can transmit a market shock. The authors identify existing EU oversight of operational dependencies and certain AI applications, while emphasising that better exposure data and supervisory expertise are needed to keep those checks relevant. Their assessment of currently limited systemic risk from AI-driven investment strategies coexists with a reason to keep monitoring. Similar positioning matters much more once a forced seller is large relative to the market available to absorb the trade.

questions.question: Where are losses moving from shareholders to creditors?
questions.detail: Follow debt issuance, claims on future revenues and refinancing schedules for the 168 supply-chain firms and their subsidiaries. Compare the change in investment funds' absolute holdings with their portfolio share, then trace which claims bank lenders ultimately retain. This would distinguish rising leverage at borrowers from rising concentration in holders' portfolios.

questions.question: Can several institutions actually recover a critical service at the same time?
questions.detail: For each important workflow, trace the application through the model supplier and cloud region to the recovery service. Compare the promised fallback with evidence from exercises involving multiple institutions. Two contracts with different suppliers protect against a different set of failures from two demonstrably independent recovery paths.

questions.question: Does excess co-loss survive conventional explanations for common equity risk?
questions.detail: Re-estimate the fund-pair comparison after matching sector and factor exposures, leverage, liquidity and fund size, then split the sample by redemptions. Persistence during high outflows would make overlapping forced sales a more credible transmission mechanism. Similarity confined to shared technology-stock exposure would point to a different monitoring priority.

questions.question: Which companies in the high-opportunity, high-threat group are adapting successfully?
questions.detail: Compare the model's business-description scores with subsequent evidence on adoption, pricing power, margins and debt service. Repeat the portfolio calculation for directly matched issuers alone before adding sector-imputed holdings. The change would show how much the financial exposure estimate depends on broad industry assignments rather than the characteristics of individual borrowers.
